# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up settles several of the questions the earlier documents left open, and it does so mostly with the right kind of evidence. Its corrections to the re-analysis and to the meta-analysis are both well founded. Four things need attention:

- The "unplanned observation" is also contamination of the control group, and it affects the decline estimate.
- The mediation result is described more strongly in the Summary than in the body.
- The Summary's headline decline mixes two hours measures.
- One Halden figure may use the wrong baseline.

## What the report says

**Varden case-processing at 24 months.** Treated offices stayed on 30 hours. A new hours measure, system log-in time, captures unclaimed work.

| Measure | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% | +9.8% |
| Output per hour, system logs | not measured | +8.5% (CI 3.4 to 13.8) |
| Output per employee | −2.1% | −3.4% (CI −8.0 to +1.2) |

- Quality, sick days and resignations are broadly unchanged from nine months.
- A mediation analysis registered at month 11 attributes 47% of the per-hour gain to fewer meetings, 18% to reduced fatigue, and leaves 35% unexplained.
- Two control offices cut meetings on their own at month 15 and gained 4.1% per hour.

**Varden counter arm.** It was stopped at month 12. Waits were 7.3 minutes in treated offices against 4.0 in control. Restoring service would have needed 12% more staff, raising cost per contact by about 9%.

**Halden subset.** Of the 23 organisations with output records, 14 responded and 3 have reverted. Output in the reverting organisations was 88–91 when they reverted. The 11 that continued show +11.8% per actual hour, which the authors present as a survivor upper bound.

**Bearing on earlier claims.** The report rebuts the re-analysis's "entirely artifact" conclusion. It also shows that the meta-analysis's four long studies were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours.

## Arithmetic check

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 24-month output per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% |
| 24-month output per hour, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% |
| Halden continuing organisations | 0.968 / (34.9 / 40.3) | +11.8% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100 |
| Counter staffing needed to restore output | 1 / (0.83 × 1.067) | about +13%, close to the stated 12% |

## What this settles

- **"Entirely an artifact" is now clearly unsupported.** The 24-month estimate meets every standard the re-analysis set: randomised comparison, record-based output, measured hours (now including unclaimed work), and long follow-up. A gain of about 8–10% remains.
- **The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim is withdrawn on good grounds.** The design of the four long studies is exactly what I flagged as the possible problem, and they turn out to be the inflating kind.
- **Unclaimed work is small.** Logs show only about 1 point more work than timesheets.
- **The meetings imbalance concern is resolved.** Baseline meeting time was similar in treated and control offices (7.4 against 7.2 hours), so the month-six difference was not a pre-existing gap.
- **The counter-arm wait times now have a control comparison.** The arm's outcome is settled: in this setting, the scheme does not work without extra staff, and extra staff costs about 9% more per contact.

## Issues

**1. The control offices' meeting audit biases the decline estimate.** The report treats the two control offices' meeting audit as an aside. It is also contamination: it raised the control group's output per hour during months 15–24. As a rough calculation, 2 of 7 offices gaining 4.1% lifts the control mean by about 1.2% over part of that window. That alone could account for perhaps a third to a half of the 2.7-point decline on the timesheet measure. "Some fading of an initial effect" may therefore partly be "control offices improving." The authors should report the 24-month estimate with those two offices excluded, or adjusted for. More generally, the 9-month and 24-month confidence intervals overlap heavily, so the decline itself is not statistically established. The body says "consistent with some fading," which is right. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" states it as fact.

**2. The Summary overstates the mediation result.**
- **"Confirms" is too strong.** The body says the meetings pathway "survives a registered test," which is fair. The mediation estimate rests on sequential ignorability, an assumption the Limitations concede a cluster trial cannot guarantee. A likely confounder is manager quality: managers who cut meetings may also be better in other ways.
- **It is not an independent replication.** The test was registered after the meetings association had been seen in the same seven treated offices. If the 24-month mediation uses months 1–9, part of the confirming data is the data that generated the hypothesis. It shows the pattern persisting in these offices, not a replication elsewhere.
- **More office-months don't add independent units.** There are still 14 clusters, so the CI of 28–66% looks narrow for that number of units. The authors should state the small-cluster method they used.
- **Was fatigue measured at baseline?** The 9-month protocol listed no fatigue scale among its outcomes. Calendar history can be recovered after the fact, but a fatigue survey cannot. If fatigue was first measured after month 11, the "0.34 SD relative to control" has no pre-period, and the 18% share is less secure than the meetings share.

**3. The Summary's headline decline mixes measures.** "Fell from 12.5% to 8.5%" compares nine-month timesheet hours with 24-month log hours. About 1.3 points of the apparent 4-point fall is the change of measure. The like-for-like figures are 12.5% to 9.8%.

**4. The Halden subset needs two checks.**
- **The hours baseline.** The baseline of 40.3 hours is the same figure as the re-analysis's average for all 27 time-tracked organisations. The authors should confirm that it is these 11 organisations' own baseline. If not, the +11.8% is computed on the wrong denominator.
- **How the reversions are characterised.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines, which is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. Two of the three reversions fit the coverage story; the third is a discretionary-sector failure and should be reported as such.
- Non-response matters too (14 of 23 replied), on top of the survivorship the authors already acknowledge. Calling the result an upper bound remains reasonable.

**5. Gaps from the nine-month report remain.**
- **Backlog and timeliness.** These are still unreported, though output per employee has drifted to −3.4% (CI down to −8.0). Whether cases are meeting statutory deadlines is the direct test of "without loss of service."
- **The cost of overtime.** Treated offices still work about 1% more than scheduled on logs.
- **Quality.** It is still reported as raw levels rather than a difference-in-differences estimate with a CI.

## Where all five documents now leave things

| Question | Status |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain under rigorous measurement | **Found.** About 8–10% at two years in one randomised trial, consistent with the meta-analysis's rigorous subsets. |
| Gains are entirely artifact | **Not supported** |
| Durability | **Largely found to two years.** The gain persists. How much it declined is uncertain, given control contamination and overlapping CIs. Beyond 24 months is open. |
| Coverage-bound work without backfill | **Found: it fails.** Restoring service costs about 9% more per contact in this setting. |
| Mechanism: meetings | **Strongly suggested, not confirmed.** The registered test agrees, but it uses the same units and relies on an untestable assumption. |
| Mechanism: fatigue | **Minor contributor.** About 18%, pending confirmation that fatigue had a baseline measure. |
| Can reorganising without cutting hours capture the gain? | **Open.** It needs an arm that reorganises without reducing hours, which no study has had. |
| Backlog and cost in discretionary work | **Open and measurable now** |

The most useful next study would add the missing arm: offices that run a meeting audit and reorganisation without reducing hours, compared with offices that do both.

I can draft a referee report on this follow-up covering points 1–5, or write up the cross-study synthesis based on the table.
